title: Slew Rate
intro: A linear circuit's step response gets steeper in proportion to the step; a real op amp's cannot, because the current available to charge its capacitors is limited. Slewing caps large-signal speed and adds distortion (Razavi, Sections 9.9 and 9.10).

blocks.text: In a linear system the step response of a one-pole circuit is $V_0(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$, whose slope $V_0 e^{-t/\tau}/\tau$ is proportional to the final value: double the step and the slope doubles everywhere. A closed-loop op amp behaves this way for small steps. For large steps the output instead ramps with a fixed slope, the slew rate, and only near the end does the response turn exponential.

blocks.alt: Plot of output voltage against time for a buffer. A 0.2 V step gives a smooth exponential. A 1 V step first rises as a straight ramp, then curves into an exponential approach to 1 V; it lags the dashed ideal exponential for a 1 V step.
blocks.caption: Step responses of a buffer with $\tau = 10$ ns and $SR = 40\text{ V}/\mu\text{s}$. Only the large step slews.

blocks.text: Origin: in a differential pair driving $C_L$ in a buffer, a small step $\Delta V$ shifts the drain currents by $\pm g_m\Delta V/2$, and the mirror delivers $g_m\Delta V$ into $C_L$; as the output catches up the current shrinks. A big step steers all of $I_{SS}$ to one side and turns the other transistor off. The loop is then effectively open: $C_L$ charges with the constant $I_{SS}$ whatever the input, giving a ramp of slope $I_{SS}/C_L$, until the output comes close enough for the off device to turn back on. The same happens on falling edges.
Slewing is nonlinear (the output does not scale with the input), so a slewing amplifier distorts. To reproduce a sine $V_0\sin\omega_0 t$ without slewing,

items: Five-transistor OTA or folded cascode with single-ended output: $SR = I_{SS}/C_L$, independent of the PMOS current $I_P$ in the folded case.
Fully differential telescopic: each output ramps at $I_{SS}/(2C_L)$ in opposite directions, so the differential output slews at $I_{SS}/C_L$.

Capacitive-feedback amplifier ($C_1$ from input to the inverting node, $C_2$ from there to the output, no extra load): during slewing $I_{SS}$ flows through the series combination, $SR = I_{SS}(C_1 + C_2)/(C_1C_2)$.
Two-stage Miller-compensated op amp: $SR = I_{SS}/C_C$ (covered with compensation in Chapter 10).

blocks.text: In a folded cascode with $I_{SS} > I_P$, slewing turns the cascode off and drives the folding node far down, pushing the input pair and tail into triode; returning to equilibrium then needs a large swing at that node, which slows settling. Clamp transistors that conduct the excess $I_{SS} - I_P$ (or tie the folding nodes toward $V_{DD}$ through devices that are off in normal operation) limit that excursion.

Raising the slew rate for a given load means raising $I_{SS}$ and widening every device proportionally to keep the swing: power and input capacitance go up, while $g_m r_O$ and hence gain stay the same. The boundary between slewing and linear settling is fuzzy; one way to define it is the input difference at which the pair's currents differ by less than some fraction $\alpha$ of $I_{SS}$, roughly $\Delta V_G \approx \alpha I_{SS}/g_m$.

A constant-current (class-A) stage can only slew with its bias current. The cure is a stage whose available current grows during the transient. In a common-source stage with a current-source load, letting the load's gate follow the input (a complementary inverter-like push-pull stage) does this but has poor supply rejection. With differential signals available, control each PMOS load through a current mirror driven by the opposite input: when one side's input falls, its NMOS draws less and the mirrored PMOS current on that side rises. These push-pull stages are loosely called class-AB.
With tail sources $I_{SS1}$ (main pairs) and $I_{SS2}$ (mirror-control pairs) and a mirror ratio $W_4/W_8$, the differential slew rate becomes

against $I_{SS1}/C_L$ without push-pull. The mirror path also adds small-signal gain: the effective input transconductance becomes $g_{m1} + (W_4/W_8)g_{m5}$. The catch is the mirror pole $\omega_{p,X} \approx g_{m8}/C_Y$, which falls as $W_4/W_8$ rises (more capacitance for the same $g_{m8}$), and a nearby zero that cannot be placed on it. Putting a differential pair in front of such a push-pull stage gives a two-stage class-AB op amp with gain $g_{m9}(r_{O9} \parallel r_{O11})[g_{m1} + (W_4/W_8)g_{m5}](r_{O1} \parallel r_{O2})$; when the first stage steers all its current to one side, its output node jumps nearly to a rail and turns the output device on hard, so the available slewing current can far exceed the bias current.

blocks.title: Slew rate for a sine
blocks.text: An op amp must deliver a 0.5 V amplitude sine at 20 MHz. What is the minimum slew rate?

blocks.title: Folded cascode
blocks.text: A single-ended folded cascode has $I_{SS} = 200\;\mu$A, PMOS currents $I_P = 150\;\mu$A and $C_L = 2$ pF. What is its slew rate? Does $I_P$ matter?
solution: $SR = I_{SS}/C_L = 200\;\mu\text{A}/2\text{ pF} = 100\text{ V}/\mu\text{s}$; $I_P$ does not set it.
But with $I_{SS} > I_P$ the folding node collapses during slewing, slowing recovery, unless it is clamped.

blocks.title: Slew plus settle
blocks.text: A buffer has $\tau = 10$ ns and $SR = 40\text{ V}/\mu\text{s}$. A 1 V step is applied. Estimate the time to settle within 1 mV and compare with a purely linear response.
solution: Slewing lasts until the linear slope $(V_0 - V_{out})/\tau$ falls to SR, i.e. until the error is $SR \cdot \tau = 0.4$ V: after $(1 - 0.4)/0.04 = 15$ ns.
Then linear settling from 0.4 V to 1 mV: $10\text{ ns} \times \ln(400) = 60$ ns. Total about 75 ns.

blocks.title: Capacitive amplifier
blocks.text: A capacitive-feedback amplifier has $C_1 = 3$ pF, $C_2 = 1$ pF and $I_{SS} = 100\;\mu$A, with negligible extra load. Find the slew rate.

blocks.title: Push-pull gain
blocks.text: A class-AB stage uses $W_4/W_8 = 4$ and $I_{SS2} = I_{SS1}$. By what factor does the slew rate rise, and at what power cost?
solution: The control pairs double the tail current (plus mirror currents), roughly twice the power.
blocks.answer: Five times the slew rate for about twice the power.
